filo indexes
filo indexes add [DIR] [--name NAME]
filo indexes remove [DIR] [--name NAME] [-y]
filo indexes refresh [DIR] [--name NAME]
filo indexes take [DIR] [--name NAME] [-y]

  A tag index is a set of HTML pages that list the files under a directory, at
  any depth, by tag. NAME.html is the find page: pick several tags (two values
  of one key match either, different keys must all match), search names and
  directories, narrow to a directory, and preview a file before opening it.
  Behind it, pages to browse one tag at a time: the keys, a page per key of its
  values, a page per tag of its files, and the files with no tags. The links are
  relative, so the pages work on any device that syncs the directory, and
  nothing is fetched from the network.

  add declares an index on DIR (the current directory if not given) and writes
  its pages: NAME.html in DIR, and the other pages and a stylesheet in
  DIR/.NAME/ (NAME is index unless given). From then on every command that
  changes the register brings them up to date, and says nothing unless it
  cannot. Scans skip both paths.

  Filo replaces or removes only the files it wrote, and only while they are as
  it wrote them: a page edited by hand, or a file put in .NAME/, is left alone
  and reported, and the command exits 1. Move it aside, then refresh writes the
  pages again. filo indexes lists the indexes and what is wrong with each.

  remove lists what it will remove and asks first. A file that is not Filo's
  stays, and so does the directory holding it; remove then exits 1. An index on
  a drive that cannot be reached (not mounted, lost) cannot have its files
  removed: remove says so and asks whether to remove the index anyway; its
  files, should they come back, are then registered by the next scan.

  An index in a synced directory is written by one device only, so two never
  rewrite each other's pages: the one that added it, until take makes this one
  write it (after asking; pages it did not write are left alone and reported).
  On the others it is listed as written by that device, refresh refuses it, and
  remove only forgets it.

Flags
  --name NAME              add: the pages' name (letters, digits, - and _);
                           remove and refresh: which index of DIR, when it has
                           several
  -y                       remove, take: without asking
